1:
Gill notes that the famine grew still sorer in Canaan, and that this is recorded to show why a second journey was necessary. Henry finds Jacob in the character of a good master of a family, careful to provide food convenient, and reads the request for a little food as fitted to the time, since in scarcity a little must suffice and nature is content with a little. Calvin asks the harder question: how could so small a purchase have supported a household of three hundred even for a few days? He rejects the guess that Jacob had been forced to sell his servants, and supposes instead that the corn was bought only for Jacob and his children and grandchildren, the servants living, as the whole region must then have lived, on acorns, herbs and roots, wheaten bread being a luxury of the rich; Gill adopts the explanation from him, while adding that some corn must have been left for the women and children. Calvin then presses what the scarcity meant: that the man to whom God had promised the land should be denied bread in it as a stranger was a severe trial, and it is profitable for us to know such conflicts of the fathers, that we may stand with the same arms though God withhold present help.

Why Judah rather than another conducted the argument is answered the same way by Gill and by Keil and Delitzsch: Reuben had already been refused, Simeon was held in Egypt, and Levi had forfeited his father's confidence over the business at Shechem. Gill adds that Judah had an interest with his father and authority among his brethren, being prudent and able to speak. Calvin suspects that Judah overstates the case in order to extort from Jacob what he would never freely grant, though he allows that many exchanges may have passed which were not recorded, and even that Joseph may have had a formal summons served. What the long disputation shows him is how hard Jacob found the parting: hunger pressing, he contended for Benjamin as if striving for the salvation of his whole family, from which Calvin conjectures that he suspected his sons of a wicked conspiracy.

Both Clarke and Ellicott object to calling Benjamin a lad. Clarke points out that the word is not the one used of a child, and would be better rendered the youth or the young man; Benjamin was at least twenty-four, some say thirty, and had a family of his own. Ellicott puts him between twenty and thirty, takes the word in Judah's mouth for a term of affection that suits the age well enough, and disposes of the claim that he is represented as a mere boy by noting that Rebekah and Shechem are both called the same thing in Hebrew.

The pledge is where the argument turns. Keil and Delitzsch observe that Joseph had never asked directly after their father and their brother, but had forced the account out of them with the charge of spying, so that Judah's report of the interview was fair enough. Clarke gives the undertaking literally — then shall I sin against thee all my days — and reads the plea from self-preservation as a chain, since without Benjamin there is no journey, without the journey no corn, and without corn Benjamin perishes with the rest. Ellicott finds the offer more manly, and therefore more persuasive, than Reuben's talk of pledging the lives of his children, and no slight matter either, since it meant standing before his father for life as a man guilty of a grievous crime. Henry and Wesley alike see in it the evidence of a real repentance: Judah's conscience had lately smitten him for Joseph, and being unable to restore the brother he had wronged, he makes what amends the case admits by doubling his care of the other.
11:
Henry admires Jacob's persuasibleness: he would be ruled by reason though it was his inferiors who urged it, and having once said his son should not go down, he let himself be over-persuaded — no fault, Henry says, but our wisdom and duty to alter a resolution when there is good reason for it, since constancy is a virtue and obstinacy is not, and it is God's prerogative not to repent. Wesley repeats the judgment. Henry then finds prudence and justice in three provisions. The money returned in the sacks goes back with a discreet construction put upon it, that it was perhaps an oversight — honesty obliging restitution not only of what comes to us by our own fault but of what comes by another's mistake, since to keep it once the oversight is discovered is to keep it by deceit. The doubled money allows for a risen price, or a ransom for Simeon. And the present is chosen from what Canaan exported and Egypt lacked.

On that doubled money the readings differ a little. Gill thinks it doubled because scarcity had made corn doubly dear, and keeps it distinct from the restored sum as a third parcel; Clarke makes it simply the returned money together with the price of a fresh load; Keil and Delitzsch prefer second money, a further sum rather than a doubling, and Ellicott, who reports both, finds that reading confirmed by the phrase used later in the chapter.

The present itself defeats precision, and Clarke says so: after all the labour of commentators we must be content with probabilities, and of the whole list the almonds are perhaps the only article we know anything about with certainty, Canaan producing the best in the east. He canvasses resin in general for the balm, the syrup of grapes or common honey for the honey, gum storax, an ointment of myrrh, and pistachios or dates or walnuts for the nuts. Ellicott settles on grape-honey boiled down to a third of its bulk, noting that Hebron still exported it into Egypt by the camel load, and on pistachios, which will not grow in Egypt. He draws two inferences from the gift: that Canaan yielded some vegetation still, or Jacob could not have kept his cattle alive; and that the smallness of the present argues a scarcity even of fruit rather than any simple notion of Egyptian greatness. Calvin makes the same allowance, since the condition of holy Jacob was not such that he could send a royal present, and adds that fruits are not always valued at their cost.

Calvin takes the prayer that follows for a pattern: we must omit nothing that is expedient and yet rely on God, for the tranquillity of faith has no affinity with indolence, and when every means has been tried we must still ascribe nothing to our own industry. He notes too that Jacob treats the hearts of men as subject to God, whom we too seldom acknowledge as the secret governor of them. The closing words divide the rest. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch read plain resignation, Ellicott adding that the supplied words of my children only lessen the pathos of a sentence which runs, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved. Calvin canvasses several senses and inclines the same way, comparing Esther's if I perish, I perish, while suspecting that Jacob spoke as he did chiefly to work upon his sons and make them careful of their brother. Clarke alone hears something other than submission: he renders the verse as a prediction, and thinks God gave Jacob at that moment a supernatural assurance that his children would be restored to him.
15:
Henry notices that Joseph, though he had seen Benjamin, did not leave off selling corn to greet him, nor trust the business to another: employment must take place of civility in its season. Clarke reads the order for dinner as a Hebrew idiom, slay a slaying, meaning a great slaughter got ready for a great entertainment; Keil and Delitzsch note that the imperative there stands in its older form. Ellicott turns the same verse against a standing objection, that the narrator errs because the higher Egyptians and especially the priests ate no flesh: representations of feasts from this period show animal food in abundance, animals sacred in one district were freely eaten in another, and the priestly rule barred mutton, pork and fish rather than beef and goose.

The invitation frightened them. Gill notes that men who came to buy corn were not lodged in the governor's house but at an inn in the city, so the summons was itself irregular. Clarke says a guilty conscience needs no accuser, and gives the phrase they used its force from wrestling — to roll oneself upon a man once he is thrown, so as to keep him down — adding that the asses they feared to lose were no small part of the family's wealth. Henry finds them making the worst of everything, as the guilty and timorous will, and expecting to be charged as cheats who had used the hurry of the market to carry off corn unpaid for. Calvin traces the panic to conscience as well, since unless the judgment of God had tormented them there was no cause to apprehend such perfidy; and he offers an innocent construction that never occurred to them, that the governor may simply have wished to show his friends the unwonted spectacle of eleven brothers sitting at one table. Ellicott observes that they would not so much as enter the house until they had assurance.

Whether the steward knew who they were is the chapter's real division. Henry thinks not, and argues from the later scene in which no one was suffered to be present when Joseph made himself known. Calvin thinks he did, and reasons it out: the man ascribes the money not to the God of Canaan but to the particular God of their father, which an Egyptian of that nation's arrogance would never have done unless he had learned better; and Simeon had plainly been kept gently rather than as a suspected spy, which argues orders given and a confidence shared. Clarke goes further and guesses the steward was himself a Hebrew, not at liberty to reveal the matter but able to promise a happy issue. Ellicott leaves the alternative open: either Joseph instructed him what to say, or he had trained his household generally in the truths of his religion.

Henry and Wesley draw the same lesson from the answer he gave, that of what we get by deceit we cannot say God gives it us, so the words at once acquit the brothers of suspicion and silence further enquiry. Calvin makes the steward's confession the credit of his master, since Joseph, unable to correct the public superstition, at least maintained the worship of the one God within his own walls. Ellicott notes that the word for treasure means what we should call a windfall. On the smaller matters the rest are brisk. Ellicott distinguishes the travelling bags in which the silver lay from the corn sacks, and remarks that only one brother had found his money at the halt, the point being that they were a full day out before anything was noticed. And Calvin, having weighed the dinner hour and the sending of each man's portion from the host's own table rather than by the cook, breaks off on the ground that such things are trivial and not conducive to piety.
26:
Henry sees the dreams coming true by degrees: the brothers bow with the present, bow again when they report their father's health, and call him thy servant our father — a form Jacob had probably taught them. Gill adds that in this the father did obeisance through his sons, so that the sun of the second dream stooped as well. Ellicott calls the scene the literal fulfilment of the first dream of eleven sheaves, and finds a fitness in men who had come to Egypt to buy corn being figured as sheaves.

Joseph's enquiry after Jacob strikes Henry as a question fit for any old man, since we are dying daily and it is strange that we are yet alive. Clarke turns the greeting to Benjamin into a complaint about language: God be gracious to thee, my son was the ordinary address of an elder to a younger in the east, emphatic once but reduced in his own day to phrases that mean just nothing, and used even in David's time as a cloak, as when Joab kissed Amasa and stabbed him. Keil and Delitzsch hear real feeling in it, my son being paternal and fitted to Benjamin's youth, and reckon him sixteen years younger than Joseph and an infant when Joseph was sold; Ellicott makes him a child of eight or nine then and nearly thirty now, and reads the question as one of pure surprise. Henry treats the tears that followed as no disparagement to great and wise men, and notes that Joseph withdrew to shed them, since gracious weepers should not proclaim their tears.

The three tables draw out everyone. Henry sets them down to hospitality, to compliance with other people's humours — for though Joseph was lord of the land he would not force Egyptians to eat with Hebrews, generous spirits hating to impose — and to the early distance between Jew and Gentile, one table not holding them both. Keil and Delitzsch call it the Egyptian spirit of caste, which barred Joseph from eating with his inferiors and them from eating with foreigners, and cite the Greek whose knife no Egyptian would touch; Ellicott repeats the authority and observes that the word abomination proves a religious and not a merely social scruple. Clarke adds two causes of his own: that Hebrews were shepherds, and Egypt had been ruined by the shepherd kings, and that Hebrews killed and ate the animals Egypt held sacred. Calvin reads the arrangement as a lesson on pride, since a nation that separates itself must itself be pure, and superstition carries its impurity within while despising everyone else; and rather than suppose the Egyptians thought their own governor polluted, he conjectures that Joseph sat apart to keep his dignity.

The seating by age astonished them. Keil and Delitzsch say it forced on them the idea that this great man had been supernaturally enlightened about their family, and Ellicott that they must have credited him with divination, precedence being a serious matter in the east. Henry rejects the suggestion that they seated themselves by custom, since the narrative would not then have marked their wonder. On the fivefold portion the readings part. Gill and Henry take it for a test, Henry adding that the point was to see whether they would envy Benjamin his larger messes as they had once envied Joseph his finer coat, and that no one should be pressed to eat or drink to excess. Ellicott thinks it more probably dictated by simple love. Calvin, having observed that Joseph meant to remain unknown and that affection broke out beyond his purpose, defends the merriment as honourable liberality and not intemperance, so that drunkards may not plead the example of the holy fathers. Wesley is content that their cares were over and they ate their bread with joy.
